newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldovan villages' vote defies Dnestr separatists.
newsitem.headline: Moldovan villages' vote defies Dnestr separatists.

text.p: This sleepy Moldovan village, scene of fierce fighting four years ago, was again turned into a battle-ground on Sunday -- this time political.

Though located in Moldova's rebel Dnestr region that looks to Moscow, Dorotcaia and several neighbouring villages decided to defy separatist authorities there and take part in Sunday's presidential poll in the former Soviet republic.
Dorotcaia and its environs have formed an enclave loyal to the central government in Chisinau just 36 km (22 miles) away and insist on living according to Moldovan law.

Moldovan tricolor flags fly from the roofs of administrative buildings, Moldovan policemen keep order and villagers eschew the depreciated Dnestr coupon currency, preferring the more stable Moldovan leu or U.S. dollars.
The 700,000-strong Dnestr region, populated mainly by Russian speakers, broke away from Moldova in 1992 fearing the newly independent state's possible merger with ethnic kin in neighbouring Romania.

Hundreds of people were killed before an interim peace settlement was reached. The memory of the war is still fresh and for the locals the choice on Sunday was simple -- backing the candidate best placed to reunite Moldova again.
"The main thing is not to allow a new war," Irina, in her 30s, told Reuters after voting. "Moldova must be united."

Like elsewhere in Moldova, residents of Dorotcaia had to choose among nine candidates. The three main contenders, however, were President Mircea Snegur, Parliament Chairman Petru Lucinschi and Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli.
Out of some 20 local residents polled by Reuters, most appeared to favour Lucinschi. "I voted for Lucinschi because he would not allow a war," Irina said.
Lucinschi presents himself as a moderate politician who favours equally close ties with Romania and Russia.

Most of Moldova was part of Romania's Bessarabia province until it was annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940 under the Nazi-Soviet non-aggression pact. The small wine-producing republic is sandwiched between Romania and Ukraine.
"Lucinschi is close to neither Romania or Russia. He is close to the Moldovan people. Peace must come here," said Alexandra, a pensioner.
Economic aspects matter as well. Lucinschi was a senior Communist Party official in Soviet times and many value his personal contacts in Russia -- Moldova's prime supplier of fuel and energy.

"Lucinschi has connections in Russia. We are a small country and have to depend on someone. When we were close to Russia we had bread. Now we understand life was good then, but is bad now," said Climentie, a middle-aged villager.

The region's instability was highlighted in a report by the central electoral commission, which said that separatist Dnestr police had disrupted voting in one of the pro-Chisinau villages. The report could not be independently confirmed.
